subtopic: MOTION FOR PRECEDENCE-GOVERNMENT'S RIGHT TO RETAIN OFFICE
speechtext:
And, by the way, confidence in the government. These were some of the funny things that I was able to tell my constituents during the election campaign, and there are some others.
I shall deal very briefly with the constitutional situation as it appears to us to-day. When I came down to the House, I had my mind absolutely and completely made up on the question of constitutionality. After listening to the address delivered by the hon. member for West Calgary, I confess he elaborated a point that had been introduced by the

leader of the opposition and that had not previously occurred to me, that is the relation of the Prime Minister to parliament and the proceedings of parliament. One cannot help admiring the eloquence and fervour with which that point of view was emphasized. The rapidity of utterance of the hon. member for West Calgary and the distance which I was removed from him prevented me from following his argument in toto, and I have not been able to read his speech since. But in the main we recognize the point that has been raised-the place of the Prime Minister in relation to the government and the question whether the government can function in parliament as a government. I confess I have had to give very serious consideration to that point since it introduces a question that I had not previously considered. But I would have attached perhaps more importance to the argument if it had not been encumbered as it was all the way through with irrelevancy. On both sides, I admit, things have been dragged into the debate that were irrelevant, I always feel that the strength of a case is vitiated if, after one strong argument in its favour has been presented, other weaker arguments are introduced. I recall the story of a British admiral who visited a certain port and who was very much annoyed when the commander of the port did1 not receive him with the regulation number of guns. He called him on board the ship and made a most emphatic protest. "Well, sir," said the port commander, "I -had nineteen good reasons for not firing the salute. The first was-I had no powder." Well, there need be no others. If the argument as to the right of the government to function in this House is so sound, I think the case would have been strengthened if -much of this discussion had been left out. There can be no doubt about that. I admit there is force in the point that has been raised. But there is another point in this amendment that must also be considered. I refer to the following paragraph:
That the party represented in the last parliament by His Majesty's opposition secured in the sa-id election by far the largest support in the popular vote, and has substantially the largest number of members of any party in the present House of Commons.
A great deal of discussion has taken place on the question of the majority in the country' and what conclusions can be properly drawn from the results of the election. My contention is that no valid conclusion can be drawn from those results if we think only of the popular vote or of the number of members who were elected. If this is the only consideration there is simply no basis on which)

Government's Right to Office
to form a conclusion. Let us take the constituencies themselves. I know pretty well what the situation is in my own constituency; I know what the result means. But I can form no opinion as to what the vote meant in many of the other constituencies in the country because wTe have no means of adequately ascertaining the views of the people in the absence of the alternative ballot. The failure to give to the country the alternative ballot has landed us just in the position we are in to-day. I was compelled on one occasion to make pretty much the same speech in regard to the alternative vote as was made last night by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell). Recognizing therefore the fact that we have no means whereby under such circumstances the people of Canada can give adequate expression to their views, it is obvious that any conclusions we may come to may be invalid. So that numbers mean nothing. Why should it be said that the largest group in the House is entitled to the support of the House? Are numbers the only things to be considered? Surely not. Surely policies and views are to be taken into consideration in the administration of the affairs of the country. Numbers in themselves mean nothing; and if wTe go back over the records of elections in the past, in the United States at any rate,-I am not sure of the facts in relation to this country-we shall find that on more than one occasion the popular vote there was not the vote represented by the administration which was formed following the election. That has happened again and again in the United States, but I should not like to make any assertion in regard to Canada because I might be wrong. If, however, majorities mean anything, then it might be pointed out that if we are to have the people represented by majorities we should have them represented in proportion to the numbers of the elected. And hon. gentlemen to our right have absolutely repudiated the principle of proportional representation. If numbers are to mean anything, and if the argument is valid from the point of view which hon. gentlemen have raised, then let us push that argument to its logical conclusion and say that proportional representation and only proportional representation can give to the country a parliament that would meet the needs of the country and express the will of the people. I therefore put aside altogether the question of numbers; all the debate that has taken place on that point has had no weight in my mind. I have attached no great importance either to the arguments advanced opposite or to the arguments that have been brought forward on this side.
There is another question that must be considered. The argument in regard to numbers has been urged as a reason why the largest party in the House should be entrusted with the government of the country, and we are asked to state clearly and distinctly, and thereby to establish a precedent,, that such a course should be followed. As I see the matter-and I am not now speaking of the relation of the Prime Minister to the House-the situation seems to me to be this: The Prime Minister in the circumstances had the option of following one of at least two courses-although there might have been others. One of these was to advise His Excellency to call upon the leader of the opposition to form a government, which of course would have been perfectly constitutional. I cannot agree with the statement that has been made that in doing so the Prime Minister would have violated anjr trust. There again we have to disagree with hon. gentlemen. And it is the fact that these extreme statements are made on one side and on the other that causes the layman to hesitate. Why should it be considered a violation of trust if the Prime Minister, recognizing the difficulty of the situation and coming to his own conclusions as to what the circumstances indicated, had advised the Governor General to ask the leader of the opposition to form a government? Or why, on the other hand, should it be said that the course he chose to follow was unconstitutional? Either alternative was open to him. Defeated governments have met parliament again and again; why therefore should it be said that up to that point the Prime Minister would have been acting unconstitutionally? It is clear, then, that so. long as the matter is left in that uncertain state the Prime Minister might very well pursue either course. He might be right or wrong from the standpoint of policy; he might be dignified or undignified; he might be doing what was expedient or what was inexpedient: I am not discussing any of those points. But so long as the situation is as it has been in the past; so long as the responsibility is left to the Prime Minister of advising His Excellency the Governor General as to what course he should adopt, I do not see that any objection could be taken in the event of the government's choosing either alternative.
We are asked in the amendment to agree that the party represented in the last parliament by the opposition secured by far the largest support in the popular vote and has now the largest number of members of any party in the House. As a statement of fact this is true; but as a premise for a conclusion

Government's Right to Office
it must be examined very closely. And the conclusion which it seeks to convey is that the party having the largest number of vote3 must of necessity occupy the treasury benches. For my part I should have to weigh that proposition very gravely. It seems to me that if we countenanced that position, in view of the fact that we have groups in parliament and that groups are likely to remain, it would be impossible for these groups to work together in harmony, as a government until one party or the other could obtain a clear majority. For my part, I say, I should have to consider very seriously whether at this juncture we could establish such a precedent. The British constitution, as we know, is a flexible thing, subject to constant change. It is built up of usages and customs and precedent, and if we adopt the course here suggested we should be establishing a precedent which in a measure would be binding upon all future administrations.

You can put that interpretation upon it. Whether it is valid or invalid is the matter I have to decide in view of what I know of the local situation. The

conclusions of other gentlemen, might not be accurate, they not having that local knowledge.
In view of the two constitutional questions which are raised now, you cannot wonder that we should hesitate to pronounce absolutely and definitely in favour of this amendment, because as it seems to me, we might be tying ourselves to a precedent which we would not wish to establish. At the same time I am compelled to recognize the force of the arguments which have been presented so ably by the legal gentlemen in the House. I am not a legal man myself, but I delight to listen to them, and I recognize the full weight of the arguments they have presented. Still there the situation remains. I do not know whether at this time it would be wise for me to say what course I would follow should the amendment be carried, but perhaps I might go so far as to say this:	I
have endeavoured to support that legislation Which I thought 'to be good and just, and to oppose that 'legislation of which I did not approve. I shall dwell upon the matter no further at this time than to say that if this amendment is carried we all know what it means. We know that it means the calling to office of the hon. gentlemen who sit to our right. But though we have had occasion to differ with them on many points, if such a situation should arise, in view of the course I have tried to follow in the past I would have to support them on legislation which appealed to me as worthy of support, and I could only withdraw my support when they introduced legislation which, to my mind, might not come up to that standard. I would have to do that, and that would be the only position I could take in the meantime. Mr. Speaker, again I say that the considerations which have been urged have caused us to weigh very carefully and seriously the whole question which has been placed before us for decision, that is, the responsibility of carrying or defeating this amendment.
Mr. JEAN J. DENIS (Joliette): Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion), addressing himself to the Progressive party, said that the Speech from the Throne was a bid for their support. That some hon. member on the side of the government might address himself to the Progressive party, and tell them, rightly or wrongly, that the Speech from the Throne wad a bid for their support I can understand, but I cannot understand the logic of the hon. gentleman who, wishing to have the Progressive party vote against this government, tells them that they have been offered a bid-a

present or something worth while to support the government. As I say, I cannot understand the logic of the hon. gentleman any more than I can understand his reasons for uttering such very Strong and indiscreet expressions this afternoon.
The hon. gentleman says that the government holds out the threat of an election. Well, Mr. Speaker, the government is making no threat of an election. We on this side of the House are not afraid of an election, because I know that a great many hon. members on this side of the House would succeed in being returned to this House just as easily as would the hon. member for Fort William. That is not a consideration. Much less is the indemnity a consideration which should weigh in the minds of hon. members in deciding the question at issue. True it is, in a way, that we are afraid of a general election, but for this reason: This country at the present time needs peace and is not ready for a general election. We do not want an election because we believe it would be contrary to the interests of the country at large. We take that attitude for that reason and that reason alone.
Then my hon. friend says thait parliament is not the highest tribunal of the land. I cannot understand that. He says the people constitute the first tribunal. Well, the people do constitute the first tribunal, but only once every five years, or every time we have an election. After the election is over the people have nothing to do with the direction of national affairs, having by their votes entrusted such direction entirely to parliament. The members of this House are the sole representatives of the people, and constitute the sole tribunal to pass upon all questions coming before them.
I w'ould not dwell upon this issue if it were not that the hon. gentleman has tried to give a lesson from beginning to end to another hon. gentleman just as capable, just as worthy as the hon. member for Fort William himself, if not more so. I refer to the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King.
Now the hon. gentleman asks: But what about the plurality vote or the popular vote? Well, it all depends upon whose ox is gored. You can count the plurality vote in a gr .at many ways. If we had in this country the alternative vote it would be much easier to count the plurality, because then where there were three members running in a single-member constituency, each elector would have two choices, and in that way the wishes of the electors could be better known. But that was not the case in the last election, where we had about eight different programmes before the people of this country, as was stated the
Government's Right to Office
other night by the Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon), and where, as in the province of Quebec for instance there were no candidates, except one or two, who designated themselves as candidates of the leader of the opposdion, and where in many constituencies in the west there were no Conservative or no Liberal candidates running, and so on. In a case of that kind, Mr. Speaker, I say it is impossible to count the popular vote and say it was in one direction or in another.
Again, is it necessary that any government should have behind it the popular vote in order to govern the country? I say not, and there are innumerable instances in history to demonstrate that it is not necessary for a government to have behind it the popular vote in order to govern. I will give one example only, and that is the case of Ramsay MacDonald, who governed England for ten months, although at the preceding general election he did not secure even one-third of the popular vote.
The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) says that political honour and dignity should have made the Prime Minister resign. The hon. gentleman should not take it upon himself to use such language unless lie be absolutely sure that he is not mistaken, and unless it be demonstrated to this House in an unmistakable v'ay that the Prime Minister had no right to retain power and convene parliament. The hon. member for Fort William even went further in that connection, and used the word "effrontery". I would say, Mr. Speaker, that it is an affront for any hon. member to abuse the Prime Minister of this country, more especially when his charges are not well-founded. What is the charge? The hon. member says to the Prime Minister: You should have resigned; you had no right to convene parliament. I shall not go into the details of that, Mr. Speaker, but I have a witness, and a worthy witness, on the other side of the House in the person of the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) who was Minister of Justice in the former administration, and who the other day said in this House in the presence of the hon. member for Fort William-and if that hon. gentleman had been listening to his colleague he could not have failed to hear it-that it was perfectly legal and proper for the Prime Minister to convene parliament andl submit his case to parliament if he chose to do so. But the hon. member for Fort I\ illiam calls it effrontery for the Prime Minister to do so; he calls it political dishonour and an indignity.
Then he went on to say that the Tory party is the most representative group in this

Government's Right to Office
parliament. That is true, and it is not true. If the most representative group means the group that has behind it the greatest number of members, I say yes, it is true. But if the most representative group is the group vdiich can align behind itself the greatest number of members, I say it is not true. Let me give an example: Suppose that we on this side of the House were free traders, and that all the other members of the House who do not belong to the Conservative party were free traders also, but belonging to a different party. On the question of the tariff would anyone say that the Conservative party was the representative party in a case of that kind? Certainly it would not be because the two other parties combined, having the same principles on the question of the tariff, could and would unite against the Conservative party, and in that case they would become the representative party.
Suppose again that it were true, as has been charged against this government so many times, that we were in favour of a lower and lower tariff all the time. We know that the members of the Progressive group are in favour of a lower tariff. Is it not true, therefore, that on that ground we could meet and form the largest group and be the most representative group in the House, although the two groups taken separately would not be as large in numbers as the Tory party?
What is the situation? I quite realize, Mr. Speaker, that it is tedious for the House to listen time and time again to each hon. gentleman giving an exposition of all the facts which have preceded the convening of this parliament, but in order to make one's address intelligible it is necessary to go back a little further than the convening of parliament.
On the 5th of September parliament was dissolved, the election to take place on the 20th of October. At that time, leaving aside the minor parties, we had three large parties in Canada. On the 20th of October the Conservative party came out of the election the largest group, the Liberal party the next largest, and the Progressive party the third largest. At once the Conservative party made the claim that they had won the election, and that the Liberal government must submit to the decision of the people and resign. May I say in passing that these hon. gentlemen have not followed all the time at least the course which they have indicated? When the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) was speaking this afternoon, hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House said they were ready for the vote. But they were not ready for the vote last Friday. After proclaiming for two months that this govern-
ment had usurped power, when on Friday afternoon last the leader of this party in this House rose and asked for a decision on the government's stand in calling parliament, immediately the Conservative party began to hedge and jockey for position; they raised questions of procedure and delayed the proceedings to the stage we have now reached. Taking the admission of the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) I say it was perfectly proper for the Prime Minister to convene parliament and not resign. Having in mind the action of the Minister of Justice last Friday afternoon II say that immediately parliament was convened the government chose the opportunity to submit their case and asked parliament to decide whether they should continue in office any longer or not. I maintain that this action was perfectly honest and justifiable on the part of the government, and my hon. friend (Mr. Manion), to say the least, had no reason for abusing the Prime Minister as he did this afternoon, more particularly when the right hon. gentleman is absent from the House.
What is the contention of my hon. friends opposite? It is that the government should have resigned at once. To place in office whom? The Conservative party evidently. Now, Mr. Speaker, I have a little problem to submit to the House in that connection, a problem which is very simple and very clear: Supposing the government had resigned immediately after the election, or within a reasonable time-let us say two or three weeks afterwards. Supposing the Tory party had been called by His Excellency to form a cabinet. Parliament would then have been convened, and the two hundred and forty-five members who compose the five or six different parties would have come here and would have been invited to vote confidence or non-confidence in the then government. Supposing further that the Progressive party, whose affiliations and policy are nearer to the Liberal than to the Conservative party, had declared: "We will not support the Conservative party because we do not believe in their policy; the party we want to support is the Liberal party,"-what would be the consequence? The Conservative party would be defeated and another general election would be required immediately. The Progressive party might then have said to the Liberal party: What business had you to resign? Because you resigned we have been deprived of the privilege of expressing our views in this House. As it is we express our views by asking for another general election. Had you remained in power, as it was your duty to do, we would

Government's Right to Office
have supported you. You would have represented the ideas and the policies of the majority of the members of parliament and you would have, been able to carry on. That, Sir, is the situation, just as surely as daylight follows darkness. But the government are held to be wrong because they did not resign. I do not see the logic of it. The policy adopted by them, I repeat, was an honest one. It is now for parliament, composed of the duly elected representatives of the people, to declare whether or not this government should remain in office. It would have been supremely illogical had the government resigned in order to put the Conservative party in office. But the situation, in consequence of the action which the government have taken, now becomes absolutely clear and logical. What do those parties want in whose hands the fate of the government now rests? If they want a Liberal administration they can have it. If they desire a Tory administration it is also their power to obtain it. They could not have had such a choice had the Prime Minister resigned immediately after October 29. and that is why such a course would have been a supreme injustice to the people whom the members here represent and to the nation at large.
What is the. proposition now before the House? It is, if the amendment carries, purely a vote of non-confidence against the government. Is it not a vote of confidence if it does carry. I say no, and1 I repeat:	It is
a vote of non-confidence against the government if it carries, but if it does not carry it is a negative vote that has no meaning. In other words, if it does not carry the government remains in power so long as parliament wants it to remain. The government may then carry on for a day, for a week, for two weeks, for a month or for two months; and let no one forget that the government is always in the hands of parliament. It is and must remain master of the situation. That is why I say it would be illogical, it would be unjust, on the part of hon. members who belong to the Progressive party, to the Independent party, or to the Labour party, or refuse to the government the test to which they are entitled. The government have submitted to the House the Speech from the Throne. Is that satisfactory to parliament, or to the members of the majority, or is it nolt? I say it is satisfactory to hon. gentlemen on this side; but if there is another group of members to whom also it should be satisfactory it is clearly those who compose the Progressive party.
While I am on this point let- me say this:
I have no hesitation in telling my Progressive friends that in the course of the last general election the argument was raised against Liberal candidates in the province of Quebec that we had sacrificed Quebec for the west.

subtopic: MOTION FOR PRECEDENCE-GOVERNMENT'S RIGHT TO RETAIN OFFICE
speechtext: No, had sold Quebec.

subtopic: MOTION FOR PRECEDENCE-GOVERNMENT'S RIGHT TO RETAIN OFFICE
speechtext:
Yes, they went
further and said that the Liberal party had been sold to the Progressive party. Those charges were untrue. We disproved them and the people stood by us. They believed then and still believe that the Liberal party has not sold itself to the Progressive party. But there is one thing which hon. gentlemen at the other end of the chamber should not forget. It is that the Liberal party have been generous to them in the past. For example, no less than twenty-six branch railway lines have been built in the west. I believe that some branch lines might have been built in Ontario and Quebec as well. However, I want hon. gentlemen to remember that the old province of Quebec, with its Latin temper, is generous. What we have been seeking in that province-being true and faithful disciples of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and William Lyon Mackenzie King-is the unity of Canada. In order to establish unity and goodwill it was necessary for us to make concessions to other provinces, and we did so. Such has been our conduct during the past four years, and such will be our conduct if we remain in power. Such will be my conduct if we are out of .power. Our motto in Quebec is "Unity and fraternity among all the provinces in this Dominion." And it will be so much the worse for those who raise the flag at times against the province of Quebec. Of course if it is their business to do so, they may do it, but this will not cause our faith to waver. We .will remain in Quebec what we have been for the last, three hundred years; we will work in conjuction with all other people throughout the Dominion in order to achieve what I have just mentioned, namely, unity, goodwill and confraternity in this Dominion. It is with these principles in view that I, for one, during the past four years supported the government, which has given a great deal to the west. I know that they have not done any injustice to the west. And now what do they propose to do? In the same spirit as previously they Say "We have a programme in the Speech from the Throne which should satisfy all the provinces in the Dominion." In the same spirit I, for one, and my colleagues on

Government's Right to Office
this side of the House I hope, as well, will be ready to support the government in carrying out the provisions of the Speech from the Throne and in their efforts to continue the policy of goodwill in this country and satisfaction to all the provinces. But I want to tell my hon. friend that if the government .Is defeated we are relieved of those sacrifices.

subtopic: MOTION FOR PRECEDENCE-GOVERNMENT'S RIGHT TO RETAIN OFFICE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: MOTION FOR PRECEDENCE-GOVERNMENT'S RIGHT TO RETAIN OFFICE
speechtext:
My right hon.
friend the leader of the opposition, for whose ability I have the greatest respect, says "hear, hear." The people of the west may ask him what he will promise, but we know that they will not get a low tariff. If they expect a low tariff from the Tory party they will be greatly deceived. I do not say that they will get a low tariff from the present government. What they are going to get is foreshadowed in the Speech from the Throne this year. What they got in the past three years was promised in the Speech from the Throne and enacted in the statutes. I am not going to tell my hon. friends that this government has offered all things to all men, but they have offered what they could under the circumstances. The government, being the guardians of the justice which must prevail throughout all the provinces of the Dominion; being the guardians of the rights of the provinces of Quebec, British Columbia, the Maritimes and all other parts of the country, have to equalize the rights of each to determine what they can do for each. They have done this in the Speech from the Throne and I ami satisfied each province is receiving its due share. If any of the provinces are receiving more than their share, I think it must be the provinces of the west.
A very strange argument was presented by the hon. member for Ivindersley (Mr. Carmichael). He said:	"The Conservative
party has been preaching tariff in season and out of season; the Liberal party has been preaching a lower tariff, but they have not given it to the country; therefore in parliament and in legislation the two parties are pretty much the same". He says further, "If I support the Conservative government and they attempt to raise the tariff, we will be here to frustrate that attempt. They number only 116, and! we of the Progressive party will be able to prevent them raising the tariff". I am sorry the hon. member is not in his seat, but I will take care to send him a copy of Hansard to-morrow, because I want him to read my remarks. The hon. member, judging from his speech, apparently thinks that he can make pawns of both parties. If the
Liberal party will give him and his friends the golden apple from the garden of the Hesperides, then they will vote for that party; otherwise they will support the Conservative party-but always with the sword lifted ready to decapitate the Prime Minister and his cabinet if they touch the tariff.
I will say to the right hon. leader of the opposition and to hon. members opposite that there are several members on this side of the House who are in favour of moderate protection. I can say this fearlessly, because three times in three successive elections in the county of Joliette I have been elected on that platform, and if the hon. member for Kindersley thinks that when he raises his sword to decapitate the government he has placed in power he is going to have the support of every member on this side on the tariff issue, he will find he is mistaken. I do not agree with the views of the opposition in some matters, but I am not so far from them in matters of tariff. It is with no shame that I make this declaration. I made it publicly in my election.

subtopic: MOTION FOR PRECEDENCE-GOVERNMENT'S RIGHT TO RETAIN OFFICE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: MOTION FOR PRECEDENCE-GOVERNMENT'S RIGHT TO RETAIN OFFICE
speechtext:
The right hon.
leader of the opposition says "hear, hear." Let him ask his own friends in the county of Joliette if at a joint meeting of five hundred people at Crabtree Mills in my own district I did not make the exact statement that I make here to-night. I stated further that in my opinion some of our industries had not enough protection and should be given more protection. After my speech on that occasion some of my opponents came to me and said, "Now you are finished1, and your government is no good." My answer to them was: "A tariff cannot be permanent. At certain periods, say ten or fifteen years or less, the tariff must be adjusted." The tariff was adjusted several times before 1896 and in the general trend the tariff was raised. In the Laurier administration the tariff was adjusted, I think, twice. Under the last administration some adjustment was made, and under the present administration there have been adjustments. And now in the Speech from the Throne the government promise that if continued in power they will have an advisory board to deal with the tariff. Therefore, the question of tariff is one of opportunity. You must study each article manufactured in this country and find out whether or not each manufacturer has or has not the necessary protection to maintain his industry and give it a reasonable profit. I wish again to tell my hon. friends from the west that they will be sorely surprised if they think they are going

Government's Right to Office
to rule the old provinces of Quebec and Ontario on this question of tariff just because we are accused of bidding for power. Personally I am not here for power. I make a declaration which I will carry out in this parliament and it is this: that above the interests of party politics I will always place the interests of the country at large and of my own province in particular. I have been elected on that platform and upon it I intend to stand until my electors change their ideas and defeat me on that platform-but they do not seem (to be in a hurry to do so now, if the majority which I received at the last general election is any indication. I beg to move the adjournment of the debate.
